units.t: Cutting Your Everyday Bills.
Part one. The price of loyalty.
Most of us treat our household bills like the weather.
The electricity bill arrives, the phone bill comes out automatically, the insurance renews, and we just pay.
But for many of these bills, the price you pay depends partly on whether you ever ask.
This lesson is about asking, comparing and, when it's worth it, switching.
Let's start with something that surprises a lot of people.
In many industries, staying loyal costs you money.
Companies often offer their sharpest prices to attract new customers.
Meanwhile, existing customers drift onto older plans, and their prices creep up year after year.
Economists sometimes call this the loyalty penalty, or the loyalty tax.
Electricity is a clear example.

In its December 2025 report on the electricity market, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission found that households who'd been on the same plan for more than three years were paying about $221 a year more than people on newer plans.
The commission also found that more than a third of households on market offers were paying at or above the default price, which is meant to be a safety net, not a good deal.
Its advice was blunt.
The single best thing most people can do to save money is to change plans, either with their current retailer or with a new one.
Some countries have stepped in.
In Britain, the Financial Conduct Authority brought in rules from January 2022 that stop home and car insurers charging renewing customers more than they'd charge a new customer for the same cover.
Here in Australia, the job of checking still falls mostly on us, the customers.
Why do companies get away with this?
Mainly because most of us never check.
Comparing plans feels confusing and a bit boring, and the savings on any one bill don't seem huge.
But across electricity, gas, mobile, internet and insurance, a few hundred dollars here and there can add up to well over a thousand dollars a year for some households.
The good news is that you don't need to become an expert.
You need about an hour, once a year, and a simple routine.
We'll cover how to compare, and then exactly what to say when you pick up the phone.
Part two. How to compare.
Start with energy.
The Australian Government runs a free comparison website called Energy Made Easy.
If you're in Victoria, the state government runs its own, called Victorian Energy Compare.
Unlike many commercial comparison sites, these government sites don't earn a commission on the plans they show you.
Have a recent bill in front of you, because your actual usage makes the comparison much more accurate.
Your bill itself can help too.
Under rules set by the Australian Energy Regulator, energy bills must tell you if your retailer has a cheaper plan available for you.
It's often a short message near the top of the bill.
If you see it, that's your cue to call.
While you're comparing, check whether you're eligible for concessions or rebates.
Pensioners, health care card holders and some other groups can get discounts on energy bills that they don't always claim.
Your state government's energy or concessions website will list them.
It's also worth looking at how your plan charges you.
Some plans have a single price for power all day.
Others, called time of use plans, charge more in the late afternoon and evening, and less at other times.
If you have solar panels, or you can run the dishwasher and washing machine in the middle of the day or overnight, a time of use plan might suit you.
If most of your power goes on cooking, heating and screens between five and nine at night, it might cost you more.
The comparison sites can show you the difference if you enter your usage.
Next, phone and internet.
The key question here is whether you're paying for more than you use.
Check how much mobile data you actually use in a typical month, and compare that with your plan.
Many people pay for a large data allowance and use a fraction of it.
Also look at whether you're out of contract.
If your phone is paid off, you may be paying a handset price for a phone you already own.
Smaller mobile brands often use the same networks as the big companies, at a lower price.
For home internet on the NBN, check your speed tier.
If one or two people mostly browse and stream, a faster, pricier tier may not make any difference you'd notice.
Then insurance.
Home and car insurance renewals are one of the biggest places the loyalty penalty hides.
Your renewal notice should show last year's premium next to this year's, so you can see the jump at a glance.
If it has gone up sharply, get two or three quotes from other insurers before you accept it.
But compare the cover, not just the price.
Check the excess, the sum insured, and what's actually covered, such as flood or accidental damage.
A cheaper policy that doesn't cover what you need isn't a saving.
Part three. Making the call.
Here's the part many people dread, but it's usually easier than expected.
Once you have a better offer in hand, call your current provider.
You'll often be put through to someone whose job is to keep customers.
If you're driving, just listen along, and save the call for when you're parked.
Here's a simple script.
Hi, I've been a customer for a few years.
I've been comparing prices, and I've found a better deal elsewhere.
Before I switch, I wanted to see what you can do.
Can you put me on your best available plan for my situation?
Then stop talking and let them answer.
Be friendly and specific.
Name the price you've found, if you have one.
If the first person can't help, ask politely whether someone else can, sometimes called the retentions or loyalty team.
If they offer a new plan, ask how long any discount lasts, and what the price will be when it ends.
Write down the name of the person you spoke to, the date, and any reference number.
And before you agree, ask them to email you the new plan details, so you can check the price matches what you were told.
A few other questions are worth asking on the same call.
Is there a discount for paying on time, or for paying by direct debit?
Am I on the right plan for how I actually use this service?
Are there any fees I'm paying that I could avoid, such as paper bill fees or card payment fees?
Small fees can add up over a year, and they're often dropped as soon as you ask.
So when should you switch instead of staying?
If your provider won't come close to the better offer, switching is usually simple.
For energy, your new retailer normally handles the change for you, and the power doesn't go off.
For phones, you can usually keep your number, but check whether you still owe money on a handset or a contract.
For insurance, make sure the new policy starts before the old one ends, so there's no gap in cover.
If something goes wrong and you can't sort it out with the company, there are free, independent ombudsman services.
Most states have an energy and water ombudsman, the Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman handles phone and internet, and the Australian Financial Complaints Authority handles insurance.
The government's Moneysmart website also has plain guides on comparing insurance and other everyday costs.
Finally, make it a habit.
Put a reminder in your calendar once a year, perhaps a month before your insurance renews, to run through every bill.
An hour of comparing and a couple of phone calls is often one of the best paid hours of your year.
Let's recap.
Loyalty often costs money, and long-standing customers can pay hundreds of dollars more than new ones.
Use independent comparison tools like Energy Made Easy, check your renewal notices, and then call and ask for the best plan available.
If they won't match it, switching is usually easier than you think.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. According to the ACCC's December 2025 report, roughly how much more were households on electricity plans older than three years paying?
Answer. About $221 a year more.
Question two. What's the name of the Australian Government's free energy comparison website?
Answer. Energy Made Easy. Victorians can also use Victorian Energy Compare.
Question three. When comparing insurance, what should you check as well as the price?
Answer. The cover, including the excess, the sum insured and what's actually included.
That's the end of Cutting Your Everyday Bills. See you on the next one.
